Open WebUI has "a rather unique combination of advanced features (RAG integrations, workspaces, pipelines, code execution, MCP integration, etc.) and a user-friendly 'production grade' interface." The commenter built a dependency on these features and is now trying to figure out where to migrate, "with no obvious alternatives."

Main gripe: the "(exorbitant) size of the docker containers," especially when you only need a gateway to third-party APIs and no local models. The new license is described as another, more serious, problem.
"It's RAG never worked for me tbh. I thought it was simply because I didn't have Gpu."

Couldn't get RAG working without a GPU either, using only external APIs. The commenter notes it pulls in all the heavy dependencies even with local compute flags disabled, so this seems to be a poorly supported case.
Commenter sees Open WebUI as "the most popular, most full-y featured OSS project" in its category, but doubts it will stay that way after moving away from a permissive license, given competitors.

"I use Open WebUI a lot, but it's lacking in a few aspects (UI, huge Docker images), and its focus on commercialization does not motivate me to contribute." The commenter asks for truly open-source self-hosted alternatives.

Called the new license "a real mess": custom clauses tacked onto BSD-3. "The fact that this is Open WebUI's second license change this year should be a red flag for anyone considering contributing to or relying on their software."

Read literally, the new license says both "don't use our branding to endorse your fork" and "don't remove our branding from your fork." The commenter argues the only way to satisfy both is not to fork. They also note the new clauses weren't formatted to 80 columns, making the license hard to read on GitHub.

Open WebUI swapped MIT for BSD-3 five months before this change, apparently without announcement; Nixpkgs and AUR still list older releases as MIT. After reading the developer's blog, the commenter concluded the change "isn't really about the community."

Users who built Open WebUI into their systems as a frontend may feel rugpulled by the license change. The suggested options are to fork and backport changes, or "bite the bullet and switch to LibreChat which is MIT licensed."
"Cool program! But... Couldn't this be a SPA running in file storage? Why do I have to install docker on a client that wants to use this? This makes it not very portable."

Calls the project name so generic it's "impossible to find documentation." Also says the project is "janky and hard to work with," and that the official docs are "LLM slop," so the only way to understand settings has been asking another LLM.

Argues OpenWebUI-style ChatGPT-lite interfaces are bad UX for local LLMs because they hide sampler settings and chat templates. Prefers prosumer tools like oobabooga, SillyTavern and ComfyUI, saying users miss features like better sampling (min_p).
"I hoped that someone would fork OpenWebUI before the license change an maintain a OSS Version," like Valkey for Redis or OpenSearch for Elasticsearch.
